## Where we are going

::: {.objectives}
**By the end of today you will be able to**

1. State the four components of the movement-ecology paradigm
2. Name the ecological drivers of movement and the trade-offs between them
3. Pick a tracking technology for a given species, question and budget
4. Explain what a *fix* is, and how the fix interval shapes the path you see
5. Load a real GPS track in R and find its gaps
:::

# 1 · Why movement matters {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Movement is the link between an animal and its environment

Almost every process a conservation biologist cares about is a movement
process in disguise:

::: {.incremental}
- **Gene flow** — dispersal distances set population connectivity
- **Disease spread** — contact rates are an outcome of where animals go
- **Population persistence** — can individuals reach the next patch?
- **Human–wildlife conflict** — where do animals and people overlap, and when?
- **Protected-area design** — a reserve that does not contain the movements
  it was drawn for does not work
- **Climate response** — range shifts are dispersal events, one individual at a time
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
If you cannot describe how an organism moves, you cannot predict how it will
respond to a changing landscape.
:::

---

## The data deluge

![Trend of "movement-related" package downloads from CRAN](../../assets/figures/cran_movement_packages.jpg){width="72%" fig-align="center"}

The constraint has moved. It used to be *getting* locations. It is now
*knowing what to do with them*.

---

## The movement ecology paradigm

Nathan *et al.* (2008) reduced the whole field to **four questions** about
every movement path:

::: {.incremental}
1. **Why move?** — the *internal state*. Hunger, thirst, reproduction, fear.
   The motivation.
2. **How to move?** — the *motion capacity*. Legs, wings, fins; the
   biomechanical envelope.
3. **When and where to move?** — the *navigation capacity*. Memory, senses,
   cues, orientation.
4. **What external factors?** — the environment. Landscape, weather,
   predators, other individuals, people.
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
$U_t = f(\Omega, \Phi, r_t, w_t)$ — the observed path is the *joint outcome* of
all four. This is why a track is hard to interpret: many different
combinations produce similar-looking paths.
:::

---

## Our spine for eight weeks

::: {.paradigm}
[Internal state]{.pbox .on}
[Motion capacity]{.pbox .on}
[Navigation capacity]{.pbox .on}
[External factors]{.pbox .on}
[Movement path]{.pbox .path .on}
:::

Each session opens with this diagram, lit up where that session's methods
speak. Tracking data record only the **bottom box**. Every method in this
course is an attempt to reason *upwards* from the path to the boxes above it.

---

## Why move? The ecological drivers

::: {.incremental}
- **Foraging** — resources are patchy and deplete; staying costs as much as leaving
- **Dispersal** — leaving the natal area: avoids inbreeding and competition with kin
- **Migration** — seasonal, round-trip tracking of resources across large distances
- **Predator avoidance** — moving away from risk, or towards refuges
- **Reproduction** — finding mates, defending territories, provisioning young
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
These map onto different *scales* of movement: foraging steps in minutes,
dispersal once in a lifetime, migration once a year. The same animal does all
of them — which is why one trajectory usually hides several processes.
:::

---

## Movement is a trade-off

Every movement decision balances **gain** against **cost**:

::: {.incremental}
- **Energy** — travelling costs calories; a richer patch further away may not pay
- **Risk** — the best food is often where predators are; the *landscape of fear*
  (Laundré et al. 2001) can matter as much as the landscape of food
- **Information** — exploring costs now but may pay later
- **Time** — a day spent travelling is a day not spent feeding or breeding
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
When a model says an animal "selects" a habitat, it is summarising the net
outcome of all these trade-offs. Sessions 7 and 8 are about disentangling
them.
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
After wolves returned to Yellowstone, elk in wolf-rich areas made less use of
aspen stands, a key forage (Fortin et al. 2005). Assuming the forage itself
did not change, which component of the paradigm explains the shift?

- [ ] Motion capacity
- [ ] Navigation capacity
- [x] External factors — acting through the animals' internal state (fear)
- [ ] None; this is a habitat-quality effect

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Forage did not change, so the habitat itself did not change. What changed was
**predation risk** — an external factor — which altered the elk's internal
state and therefore the trade-off between food and safety. This is the
*landscape of fear* idea.

It also shows why the four components cannot be read separately: the same
external change works through the animal's internal state. It is also why a
habitat-selection model fitted before and after wolf reintroduction would give
different coefficients for the same, unchanged vegetation.
:::
:::

---

## Lagrangian vs Eulerian

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Lagrangian
**Follow the individual.**

Telemetry, biologging, mark-recapture.

*"Where did animal #7 go?"*

Gives you the **process**: the sequence of decisions.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Eulerian
**Watch a fixed place.**

Camera traps, transects, counts, eDNA.

*"How many animals passed this point?"*

Gives you the **pattern**: density in space.
:::
:::

. . .

This course is almost entirely **Lagrangian** — but remember the two are
linked: a distribution is what you get when you integrate movement over time.

---

## Vocabulary — get this right now
| Term | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| **Fix** (or *relocation*) | One estimated location **with a timestamp**. The atom of everything. |
| **Track** / **trajectory** | An ordered sequence of fixes for **one individual** |
| **Burst** | A stretch of a track with regular sampling and no big gaps |
| **Step** | The straight segment between two consecutive fixes |
| **Step length (SL)** | Distance of a step. Note: **not** distance travelled |
| **Turning angle (TA)** | Change of direction between consecutive steps |
| **Fix rate** / sampling interval | How often the tag tries to locate |
| **Fix success rate** | Fraction of attempts that produced a location |
| **Deployment** | One tag, on one animal, over one period |

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
A track is **not** the path the animal walked. It is a *sample* of that path.
Everything between two fixes is an assumption.
:::

---

## The vocabulary, in one picture

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-align: center
fx <- c(0, 1.6, 2.4, 4.0, 4.6, 8.2, 9.4, 10.2, 11.8)
fy <- c(0, 0.9, 2.4, 2.8, 1.6, 1.0, 2.2, 0.8, 1.4)
burst <- c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2)
set.seed(3)
true_x <- spline(seq_along(fx), fx, n = 200)$y + rnorm(200, 0, 0.06)
true_y <- spline(seq_along(fy), fy, n = 200)$y + rnorm(200, 0, 0.06)

par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(fx, fy, type = "n", asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     xlim = c(-0.5, 12.3), ylim = c(-1, 3.6))
lines(true_x, true_y, col = faint, lwd = 2, lty = 3)
for (b in 1:2) lines(fx[burst == b], fy[burst == b], lwd = 4, col = c(teal, gold)[b])
segments(fx[5], fy[5], fx[6], fy[6], lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = rust)
text((fx[5] + fx[6]) / 2, (fy[5] + fy[6]) / 2 - 0.45, "gap: no step across it", col = rust, cex = 1.5)
points(fx, fy, pch = 21, bg = "white", cex = 2.6, lwd = 3)
# a step length and a turning angle
text(0.55, 0.85, "step", cex = 1.5, srt = 29)
h1 <- atan2(fy[3] - fy[2], fx[3] - fx[2]); h0 <- atan2(fy[2] - fy[1], fx[2] - fx[1])
segments(fx[2], fy[2], fx[2] + 1.1 * cos(h0), fy[2] + 1.1 * sin(h0), lty = 3, lwd = 2)
a <- seq(h0, h1, length.out = 30)
lines(fx[2] + 0.75 * cos(a), fy[2] + 0.75 * sin(a), lwd = 3, col = rust)
text(fx[2] + 1.35, fy[2] + 0.75, "turning\nangle", col = rust, cex = 1.5)
text(fx[1], fy[1] - 0.5, "fix", cex = 1.5)
text(2.3, -0.75, "burst 1", col = teal, cex = 1.7, font = 2)
text(10, -0.4, "burst 2", col = gold, cex = 1.7, font = 2)
legend("topright", c("what the animal walked (unknown)", "what the track records"),
       lty = c(3, 1), lwd = c(2, 4), col = c("grey50", ink), bty = "n", cex = 1.4)
```

Nine fixes, two bursts, seven steps. The dotted path is what happened; the
straight lines are what we analyse.

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
A GPS collar is set to attempt a fix every hour. Over one day it produces 18
locations. The straight-line distances between consecutive fixes sum to 4.1 km.
Which statements are true?

- [ ] The animal travelled 4.1 km that day
- [x] The animal travelled **at least** 4.1 km that day
- [x] The fix success rate was 75%
- [ ] The 6 missing fixes can be safely ignored

::: {.quiz-feedback}
4.1 km is a **lower bound**: the animal's real path between fixes is at least
as long as the straight line, and usually much longer. Summed step length is
scale-dependent — sample twice as often and it grows.

18/24 = 75% success. And the missing fixes are the opposite of ignorable:
GPS failures are *not random*. Fixes fail under canopy, in gorges, in dense
cover — exactly the habitats an animal may be selecting. Missing data are
themselves an ecological signal.
:::
:::

# 2 · How we track animals {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## The toolbox, from cheapest to most expensive

| | Method | Locations? | Typical cost |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 🏷️ | Marks & recapture | Two points, maybe | € |
| 📻 | VHF radio-telemetry | Human-limited | €€ |
| 🛰️ | Argos (Doppler) | 250 m – 10 km | €€€ |
| 📡 | GPS store-on-board | 5–30 m | €€€ |
| 📱 | GPS + GSM / Iridium | 5–30 m, live | €€€€ |
| 💡 | Light-level geolocators | ~100–200 km | €€ |
| 📈 | Accelerometers / IMU | No — *behaviour* | €€ |
| 🔊 | Acoustic telemetry | Receiver range | €€€ |

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
There is no best technology. There is only the best technology **for this
animal, this question, and this budget** — and the animal's body mass usually
decides for you.
:::

---

## Marking individuals: the cheap and enduring methods

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![*Cyclura carinata* with coloured bead tags](../../assets/figures/iguana_beads.jpg){width="100%"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![A Passive Integrated Transponder (PIT)](../../assets/figures/pit_tag.jpg){width="100%"}
:::
:::

Marks give you **recaptures**, not tracks — two or more points separated by a
long, unobserved interval. Cheap, long-lasting, and still the backbone of
demographic work.

---

## Marking: from mutilation to photographs

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
![Toe-clipping combinations (Waichman 1992)](../../assets/figures/toe_clipping.jpg){width="100%"}

Effective, permanent — and now ethically contested. Increasingly replaced.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![*Bombina* spot patterns are unique](../../assets/figures/morpho_pattern.jpg){width="100%"}

Natural markings cost the animal nothing. Photo-ID software now does the
matching at scale.
:::
:::

---

## Photo-identification at scale

![Automated recognition of individual iguanas. Image courtesy of Nathalie Duporge](../../assets/figures/photo_id_software.jpg){width="62%" fig-align="center"}

Pattern-matching algorithms turn a shoebox of photographs into a
capture–recapture dataset — for whale sharks, giraffes, newts, iguanas.

---

## Genetic tagging

![Species and locations where genetic tagging has delivered demographic insight (after Lamb et al. 2019)](../../assets/figures/genetic_tagging.jpg){width="66%" fig-align="center"}

Hair snags, scats, feathers: the animal is never handled. Biased towards
mid-to-large mobile mammals, because that is where the money and the conflict are.

---

## VHF radio-telemetry

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Implanted transmitter, *Chilabothrus chrysogaster*](../../assets/figures/boa_transmitter.jpg){width="100%"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Tracking on foot with a Yagi antenna](../../assets/figures/vhf_antenna.jpg){width="100%"}
:::
:::

The tag emits a pulse; **you** find it. A location comes from *homing in* or
from **triangulation** of ≥2 bearings. Tags go down to **0.2 g** — nothing
else reaches insects and the smallest bats.

---

## What triangulation actually costs you

::: {.incremental}
- Each bearing has error; the location error is the **intersection polygon**
  of two noisy bearings, and it grows fast with distance
- Data arrive **when a human is in the field** — so nights, storms and
  weekends are systematically under-sampled
- A few dozen to a few hundred fixes per animal, unevenly spaced
- Cheap tags, expensive *fieldwork*
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
The bat dataset we will use in Session 3 is exactly this: 17 individuals,
1,740 fixes *in total*, wildly irregular. Most methods in this course assume
regular sampling. Part of your training is learning to say **"not with these
data"**.
:::

---

## GPS: trilateration

![The GPS constellation](../../assets/figures/gps_constellation.gif){width="42%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.incremental}
- Each satellite broadcasts its position and a very precise time
- Distance to a satellite = (signal travel time) × c
- **3 satellites** fix a position in principle; a **4th** is needed to solve
  the receiver's clock error — and more give altitude and redundancy
:::

---

## GPS in practice, on an animal
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**What you get**

- Horizontal error typically **5–30 m** under open sky
- A quality flag: number of satellites, **DOP** (dilution of precision), 2D vs 3D fix
- Optional altitude, speed, temperature, activity

**What it costs**

- A **cold start** (no recent almanac) can take minutes and drain the battery
- Canopy, canyons, burrows and water block the signal
- Energy scales with fix rate — this is the central design trade-off
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![A male *Conolophus marthae* with a Wireless Sensor Node: GPS, temperature and UV](../../assets/figures/iguana_wsn.jpg){width="100%"}
:::
:::

---

## Getting the data off the animal

::: {.incremental}
- **Store-on-board** — cheapest, best battery use, but you must **recapture**
  the animal. Lose the animal, lose everything.
- **VHF/UHF download** — get close, pull the data over the air
- **GSM / SMS** — near-live data wherever there is mobile coverage. Fails in
  exactly the remote places you care about.
- **Iridium / Argos uplink** — global, live, expensive, small data volumes
- **Drop-off collars** — timed or remotely triggered release, then go and find
  the collar. Elegant, and one more thing that can fail.
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Ask *"how will I get the data back?"* **before** you buy the tags. This is the
question most first projects get wrong.
:::

---

## Argos, geolocators, and the aquatic world
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Argos
Satellites measure the **Doppler shift** of the tag's transmission.

Error classes 3 → B: **~250 m to >10 km**.

Global, works at sea, decades of history. Still standard for sea turtles,
seabirds, pinnipeds.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Geolocators (GLS)
Log **light level**. Day length → latitude; time of local noon → longitude.

Error **100–200 km**. Useless near equinox.

But: ~0.3 g. For small migratory birds it is the *only* option.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Acoustic telemetry
Tag pings; **fixed hydrophones** listen.

You get detections at receivers, not positions — a **network** problem,
not a trajectory problem.

Fish, sharks, invertebrates.
:::
:::

---

## Biologging: sensors that are not locations

::: {.incremental}
- **Tri-axial accelerometers** — the workhorse. At 10–50 Hz you can classify
  feeding, resting, flying, and estimate energy expenditure (ODBA)
- **Magnetometers + gyroscopes** — heading and body rotation; combined with
  accelerometers gives **dead reckoning**: a fine-scale path between GPS fixes
- **Pressure / depth** — dive profiles
- **Temperature, heart rate, gut temperature** — physiology in the wild
- **Proximity tags** — who was near whom, and for how long: social networks
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
The frontier is not more locations. It is **locations plus sensors**: knowing
*where* **and** *what the animal was doing there*. Session 8 is the statistical
version of this question when all you have is the trajectory.
:::

---

## Archival tags and camera traps

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Archival tags
Store everything on board — depth, temperature, light, acceleration — for
months or years. No transmission, so tiny and long-lived.

The catch: **you only get the data if you get the tag back**. Pop-up archival
tags on fish detach and float to the surface to transmit a summary.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Camera traps
Eulerian, not Lagrangian: they watch a place, not an animal.

But they are the natural **complement** to tracking — who else uses the
places your collared animals use, when, and how often? Occupancy and
spatial capture–recapture models connect the two worlds.
:::
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
You must study the migratory route of a 22 g passerine that breeds in Italy
and winters somewhere in sub-Saharan Africa. Individuals return to the same
nest box each spring. Which technology?

- [ ] GPS/GSM collar
- [x] Light-level geolocator
- [ ] Argos PTT
- [ ] VHF radio-telemetry

::: {.quiz-feedback}
The **5% rule** decides it: the tag should stay under ~5% of body mass, so
~1.1 g here. That excludes GPS/GSM and Argos PTTs outright. VHF has no
transcontinental range.

A geolocator weighs a few tenths of a gram. Its 100–200 km error would be
useless for home-range work but is irrelevant for a 4,000 km migration.

And crucially: geolocators are **store-on-board**, so the whole design depends
on the birds' nest-box philopatry — you must **recapture** them. That is not a
detail, it is the study.
:::
:::

---

## Choosing: the trade-off table
| | Accuracy | Min. mass | Data return | Temporal coverage |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Marks / PIT | Point of capture | ~0.1 g | On recapture | Sparse |
| VHF | 10s–100s m | **0.2 g** | Manual, live | Human-limited |
| Geolocator | 100–200 km | **0.3 g** | On recapture | Continuous |
| Argos | 250 m – 10 km | ~5 g | Remote, global | Good |
| GPS store-on-board | 5–30 m | ~1 g | On recapture | Programmable |
| GPS + GSM | 5–30 m | ~15 g | Remote, live | Programmable |
| Accelerometer | — (behaviour) | ~0.5 g | Usually on recapture | Very high rate |

::: {.keyidea}
Read this table **right to left**. Start from "how do I get the data back and
how much does the animal weigh", not from "what accuracy would be nice".
:::

---

## Which tags can this animal carry?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| fig-align: center
tags <- data.frame(
  tech = c("PIT", "VHF", "Geolocator", "Accelerometer", "GPS store-on-board", "Argos", "GPS + GSM"),
  g    = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1, 5, 15))
animals <- c("passerine 22 g" = 22, "kestrel 200 g" = 200, "fox 6 kg" = 6000,
             "buffalo 600 kg" = 6e5)
par(mar = c(4.6, 15, 1, 1), cex.axis = 1.35, cex.lab = 1.6, las = 1)
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 1e6), ylim = c(0.5, nrow(tags) + 0.5), log = "x", axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "Body mass of the animal", ylab = "")
axis(1, at = 10^(0:6), labels = c("1 g", "10 g", "100 g", "1 kg", "10 kg", "100 kg", "1 t"))
axis(2, at = seq_len(nrow(tags)), labels = tags$tech, tick = FALSE)
abline(v = animals, col = faint, lwd = 2)
text(animals, nrow(tags) + 0.45, names(animals), pos = c(2, 4, 4, 2), cex = 1.2, col = "grey40")
segments(tags$g / 0.05, seq_len(nrow(tags)), 1e6, seq_len(nrow(tags)), lwd = 14, col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.5), lend = 1)
segments(tags$g / 0.03, seq_len(nrow(tags)), 1e6, seq_len(nrow(tags)), lwd = 14, col = teal, lend = 1)
```

Bars: animals heavy enough for each tag under the 5% rule (light) and the 3%
rule for flyers (dark). The 22 g passerine of the quiz can carry a PIT, VHF,
geolocator or accelerometer — nothing that transmits a position.

# 3 · Doing it responsibly {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Tag effects are real

::: {.incremental}
- The **3–5% rule** (tag ≤ 3% of body mass for flying animals, ≤ 5% for
  terrestrial ones) is a *convention*, not a finding. Portugal & White (2018)
  showed miniaturisation has not made published studies lighter relative to
  body mass — researchers just tag smaller animals.
- For flying and diving animals, **drag and shape matter more than mass**.
  A streamlined 3% package can beat a bluff 1.5% one.
- Documented effects: reduced breeding success, higher energy expenditure,
  altered diving, changed social status, injury at the attachment site.
- Effects are often **delayed** — and studies are rarely designed to detect them.
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
A tagged animal is, to some degree, a *modified* animal. The honest position
is to minimise, measure and report the effect — not to assume it away.
:::

---

## Ethics and permits: the checklist

::: {.incremental}
1. **Is the question worth it?** Would existing data answer it?
2. **3 Rs** — replace, reduce, refine. The smallest sample that can answer the question.
3. **Ethics approval** and national/regional permits, *before* fieldwork.
   In Italy: ISPRA and regional authorisations; EU Directive 2010/63 where applicable.
4. **Capture and handling** protocol, anaesthesia where required, trained personnel.
5. **Attachment** — weak links and planned drop-offs so nothing is worn forever.
6. **Data sensitivity** — for poached species, publishing exact coordinates can
   be lethal. Movebank supports embargo and coarsening.
7. **Report the effects you observed**, including the animals you lost.
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
Which of these is the *strongest* argument for choosing a 30-minute fix
interval over a 5-minute one, for a study of buffalo habitat selection?

- [ ] 30-minute data are more accurate
- [x] It extends the deployment over a whole year, capturing seasonal variation
- [ ] Statistical software cannot handle 5-minute data
- [ ] 30 minutes is the standard for ungulates

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Fix interval is a **battery** decision, and therefore a decision about *how
long* you observe. 5-minute data over six weeks and 30-minute data over a year
answer different questions — and for seasonal habitat selection, the year wins.

Accuracy per fix does not change with rate. Software is not the constraint.
And "it's the standard" is never a reason — it is a description of what other
people's batteries could manage.

The real cost: coarse sampling **truncates** the step-length distribution.
You will see this bite in Sessions 4 and 7.
:::
:::

# 4 · Sampling design {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## The fix interval decides what path you see

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
source("R/simulators.R")
set.seed(8)
true_path <- simulate_crw(2880, shape = 2, scale = 15, kappa = 1.2)  # 1 fix/min, 2 days
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
for (k in c(1, 60, 360)) {
  d <- true_path[seq(1, nrow(true_path), by = k), ]
  len <- sum(sqrt(diff(d$x)^2 + diff(d$y)^2)) / 1000
  plot(true_path$x, true_path$y, type = "l", col = "grey85", asp = 1,
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  lines(d$x, d$y, col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2)
  points(d$x, d$y, pch = 16, cex = if (k == 1) 0 else 0.9, col = "#1f6f78")
  title(sprintf("every %s — path %.0f km",
                c("1" = "minute", "60" = "hour", "360" = "6 hours")[as.character(k)], len),
        cex.main = 2)
}
par(op)
```

The **same** two days of simulated movement (grey), sampled at three rates.

---

## The modifiable temporal unit problem

The spatial version is famous in geography (Openshaw 1984): results change
with the size of the spatial units you aggregate into. Tracking has its own
temporal version.

::: {.incremental}
- **Path length** shrinks as the interval grows — every straight segment cuts
  corners the animal actually walked
- **Speed** is really *distance per interval*: the same animal is "slower"
  when sampled more coarsely
- **Tortuosity** and **turning angles** change — fine sampling shows wiggles,
  coarse sampling shows randomness
- **Behaviours shorter than the interval become invisible**
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
There is no "true" speed or step length independent of the fix interval. Choose
the interval from the **question**, and never compare metrics across studies
sampled at different rates.
:::

---

## Designing a deployment

Four numbers you fix before the first capture:

::: {.incremental}
1. **Fix interval** — set by the fastest behaviour you need to resolve
2. **Duration** — set by the slowest process (seasonal selection needs a year)
3. **Number of animals** — set by the *population* question; individuals vary
4. **Battery** — the budget that forces 1 × 2 × 3 into a compromise
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Interval × duration × number of animals ≈ constant for a given budget. A study
of foraging decisions and a study of seasonal range shifts need different
collars, or at least different schedules.
:::

---

## One battery, many designs

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
budget <- 8000                                         # fixes one battery can deliver
interval_h <- c("every 5 min" = 5 / 60, "every 30 min" = 0.5, "every hour" = 1, "every 4 hours" = 4)
days <- budget * interval_h / 24
slide_par(mar = c(4.6, 12, 1, 1))
bp <- barplot(rev(days), horiz = TRUE, col = teal, border = NA, xlim = c(0, 1600),
              xlab = "Deployment (days)", names.arg = rev(names(days)))
text(rev(days), bp, c("3.7 years", "11 months", "5.5 months", "4 weeks"), pos = 4, cex = 1.5)
```

An illustrative battery worth 8,000 fixes. Fine sampling buys detail and costs
duration — nearly a month at 5 minutes, nearly a year at 1 hour.

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
You compute a buffalo's daily travel distance from hourly fixes and get 4 km.
A colleague using the same collars set to fix every 5 minutes reports 9 km for
the same population. What is the most likely explanation?

- [ ] The colleague's collars were less accurate
- [x] Finer sampling captures more of the path's tortuosity, so summed distance grows
- [ ] The populations behave differently
- [ ] Hourly fixes over-estimate distance

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Summed step length is a **lower bound** on the distance travelled, and the
bound tightens as sampling gets finer: every hourly step cuts across the
wiggles that 5-minute fixes capture. More than doubling is entirely normal.

There is a second, smaller effect working the other way: at very fine
intervals GPS error adds spurious zig-zag, inflating distance. That is why the
"right" interval is not simply "as fine as possible".

Neither 4 km nor 9 km is *the* daily distance. Each is a daily distance **at a
given sampling interval**, and must be reported that way.
:::
:::

# 5 · The three biases {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Bias 1 — Fix success is not random

::: {.incremental}
- GPS fixes fail under **dense canopy**, in **steep terrain**, in **burrows**,
  underwater
- So the fixes you *have* are biased towards open habitat
- Then you fit a habitat-selection model and conclude the animal prefers
  open habitat
- **You have measured your collar, not your animal**
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Fixes are missing *because of* the covariate you are modelling. This is
missing-not-at-random, the nastiest kind. Mitigation: stationary test
collars in each habitat type, and model fix success explicitly.
:::

---

## Bias 2 — Location error is structured

::: {.incremental}
- Error is **not** independent white noise: it is correlated in time and
  correlated with habitat
- A bad fix can place an animal hundreds of metres away, producing an
  implausible step out and an implausible step back — a **spike**
- Naïvely, that spike inflates your speed distribution and your home range
- Filtering on speed is the standard fix, but a threshold that is too
  aggressive deletes real fast movement
:::

. . .

Keep the DOP / satellite-count columns. They are your evidence about which
fixes to distrust. We use them in Session 3.

---

## Bias 3 — The sample of animals

::: {.incremental}
- Tagged animals are the ones you could **catch**: often bolder, often in
  accessible places, often adults, often one sex
- Sample sizes are small — 6 buffalo, 1 vulture. Individual variation is
  large, and $n=1$ tells you about *that individual*
- Tags fail unevenly: animals in rough habitat lose collars more often,
  so late in a study your sample has drifted
- Publication bias: dispersal studies report the animals that were *found*
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Three questions for every tracking paper you read, including yours:
**Which animals? Which fixes? What is missing, and why?**
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
A study reports that collared deer "avoid dense forest", based on GPS collars
with an overall fix success of 62%. What is the first thing you should check?

- [ ] Whether the sample size was large enough
- [x] Whether fix success itself differed between forest and open habitat
- [ ] Whether the collars were calibrated
- [ ] Whether the study was peer-reviewed

::: {.quiz-feedback}
A 38% failure rate is enormous, and canopy is the classic cause of GPS
failure. If the collar fails more often under trees, forest locations are
under-represented in the data *by construction* — and "avoidance" is an
artefact of the instrument.

Sample size does not help: more collars with the same bias give you a more
precise wrong answer. The standard remedy is stationary test collars deployed
across habitat types to estimate habitat-specific fix rates, then weight or
model accordingly.
:::
:::

# 6 · Where the data live {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Movebank

[movebank.org](https://www.movebank.org) — the field's shared repository.

::: {.incremental}
- Thousands of studies, billions of locations; many openly licensed
- A **controlled vocabulary**: `timestamp`, `location-long`, `location-lat`,
  `individual-local-identifier` — always the same names, always UTC, always WGS84
- **Env-DATA**: upload a track, get it annotated with weather, NDVI, land
  cover, elevation. We do this by hand in Sessions 2–3 so you understand what it does.
- R access through the `move2` package
:::

. . .

Our three datasets all come from there — see the [Datasets page](../../data.qmd).

---

## Meet the animals

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
library(sf)
buf <- read_buffalo()
leo <- read_leo()
bat <- read.csv("data/bat_safi.csv.gz")
bat <- bat[!is.na(bat$location.long), ]
world <- spData::world

par(mfrow = c(1, 3)); par(cex = 1); map_par(cex.main = 1.5)
# a handful of corrupt fixes lie tens of km away (Session 3); keep the map on the herds
buf <- buf[buf$x > quantile(buf$x, 0.001) & buf$x < quantile(buf$x, 0.999) &
           buf$y > quantile(buf$y, 0.001) & buf$y < quantile(buf$y, 0.999), ]
ids <- unique(buf$id); bcols <- hcl.colors(length(ids), "Dark 3")
plot(buf$x, buf$y, type = "n", asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     main = "6 buffalo, Kruger NP")
for (i in seq_along(ids)) with(buf[buf$id == ids[i], ], lines(x, y, col = bcols[i], lwd = 0.7))
scale_bar(20)

laea <- "+proj=laea +lat_0=30 +lon_0=-90"
leo_xy <- sf_project("EPSG:4326", laea, cbind(leo$lon, leo$lat))
plot(st_geometry(st_transform(world, laea)), col = "grey93", border = "grey70",
     xlim = range(leo_xy[, 1]) + c(-5e5, 5e5), ylim = range(leo_xy[, 2]) + c(-3e5, 3e5),
     main = "Leo, turkey vulture, 2007–2013")
gap <- c(FALSE, diff(as.numeric(leo$t)) > 3 * 86400)     # do not draw across data gaps
leo_xy[gap, ] <- NA
lines(leo_xy, col = rust, lwd = 0.8)

utm32 <- st_transform(world[world$name_long == "Switzerland", ], 32632)
bat_xy <- sf_project("EPSG:4326", "EPSG:32632", cbind(bat$location.long, bat$location.lat))
plot(st_geometry(utm32), col = "grey93", border = "grey70",
     main = "17 bats, VHF, Switzerland")
points(bat_xy, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.7))
scale_bar(50)
```

Hourly GPS on a resident grazer; six years of GPS on a migrant crossing two
continents; a few hand-collected VHF fixes per bat per night.

## Recap

::: {.incremental}
- The **paradigm**: internal state, motion capacity, navigation, external
  factors → path. We only ever observe the path
- Animals move to forage, disperse, migrate, avoid predators and breed — each
  a trade-off between gain and cost
- Technology choice is driven by **body mass** and **data recovery**; the
  3–5% rule is a convention, not a guarantee
- The **fix interval** shapes the path you see — the modifiable temporal unit
  problem
- Three biases: **fix success**, **location error**, **which animals you caught**
:::

. . .
